content: The evidence regarding the effects of tender-point deep massage on pain, function, and health-related quality of life was evaluated in comparison to sham interventions. Across six trials, benefits were observed for these outcomes. However, the certainty of the evidence was very low, making it unclear whether massage had little to no effect on pain in the immediate term, reduced pain in the short term (moderate effect), or slightly reduced pain in the intermediate term (small effect). No data were available for long-term follow-up. The impact of massage on back-specific function was similarly uncertain across immediate, short, and intermediate terms, with moderate effects reported but very low certainty of evidence. Again, no data were available for long-term follow-up. Massage may improve fear-avoidance beliefs in the immediate and short terms (moderate effects, low-certainty evidence), but no data were available for intermediateor long-term follow-up. In a single trial involving older adults, the benefits of massage were uncertain due to very low certainty of evidence. The 95% confidence interval suggested that massage might make little to no difference to pain and function in the immediate and short terms. None of the included trials reported on harms. When comparing massage to no intervention, no trials were identified. In comparisons of massage with usual care (three trials), benefits were observed for pain, function, and fear-avoidance beliefs. However, the certainty of the evidence was very low, leaving it unclear whether massage had little to no effect on pain in the immediate term, reduced pain in the short term (moderate effect), or had little to no effect on pain in the intermediate term. No data were available for long-term follow-up. Similarly, it was uncertain whether massage had little to no effect on back-specific function in the immediate term, improved function in the short and intermediate terms (moderate effects), or slightly improved function in the long term (small effect). Massage may have improved health-related quality of life in the immediate term (large effect), short term (moderate effect), and intermediate term (small effect), but no data were available for long-term follow-up. One trial was retracted by the publisher in June 2023 after the meta-analyses were conducted. A sensitivity meta-analysis was performed to explore the effects on pain and function outcomes in the immediate term with and without the retracted trial included. The certainty of the evidence remained very low, and the 95% confidence interval indicated that massage might make little to no difference to back-specific function. In comparisons of massage added to another intervention versus the other intervention alone (six trials), benefits were observed for pain and function. However, the certainty of the evidence was very low, making it unclear whether massage had little to no effect on pain in the immediate term or reduced pain (small effect) in the short term. No data were available for other time points. Similarly, it was uncertain whether massage improved back-specific function in the immediate term (moderate effect) or short term (large effect), as the 95% confidence interval suggested little to no difference. No data were available for other time points. Massage appeared to make little to no difference to health-related quality of life in the short or immediate terms. In a single trial involving older adults, benefits were observed for pain. However, the certainty of the evidence was very low, making it unclear whether massage reduced pain in the short term (moderate effect) and improved health-related quality of life (moderate effect), as the 95% confidence interval suggested little to no difference. No data were available for other time points. None of the included trials reported on harms. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) noted that in six sham-controlled trials, small to moderate benefits for pain were observed in the short and intermediate terms, with moderate benefits for function in the immediate, short, and intermediate terms, and moderate benefits for fear-avoidance beliefs in the immediate and short terms. However, the GDG identified a lack of outcomes data beyond the intermediate term, raising uncertainty about the longer-term benefits and harms of massage. Harms were judged to be uncertain due to inconsistent reporting and very low certainty of evidence. Nonetheless, the GDG considered the likely benefits of massage to outweigh the risk of harms when delivered by trained health workers, as the risk of harms was judged to be low and transient. The GDG reached a consensus conditional recommendation in favor of massage based on small to moderate benefits for important outcomes, predominantly pain and function, identified in the sham-controlled trials. However, the GDG acknowledged that the certainty of evidence for benefits and harms was low to very low, and attitudes toward massage and its accessibility varied between countries. Some people might prefer manual therapies like massage due to its hands-on nature, while others might not favor this approach. Massage was judged to be associated with moderate costs, with cost and equity impacts varying by setting, particularly where massage therapies are provided outside healthcare facilities. Delivery of massage was considered feasible in most settings, although acceptability might vary across health workers and individuals with chronic primary low back pain. Regarding traction, the evidence for its benefits and harms in chronic primary low back pain was based on an updated Cochrane systematic review. Ten trials with 921 participants were included, but no trials reported outcomes for older adults separately. Most trials used motorized traction, with one trial examining underwater traction using weights. No trials used manual traction. The evidence for traction was very low certainty, and no trials reported on harms. In comparisons of traction with sham, no differences were observed for pain in the short term, and no data were available for other time points or critical outcomes. In comparisons of traction added to another intervention versus the other intervention alone (nine trials), benefits were observed for pain and function. However, the certainty of the evidence was very low, making it unclear whether traction reduced pain in the immediate (small effect) and intermediate terms (moderate effect) or made little to no difference in the short term. Similarly, it was uncertain whether traction improved back-specific function in the immediate (small effect) and intermediate terms (small effect) or made little to no difference in the short term. No data were available for long-term outcomes. The GDG judged the overall net benefits of traction to be trivial and uncertain for all adults and largely uncertain for older adults due to a lack of evidence. The GDG also identified a lack of outcomes data beyond the intermediate term, raising uncertainty about the longer-term benefits and harms of traction. Harms were judged to be uncertain due to inconsistent reporting, with some trials reporting potential harms such as aggravation of neurological symptoms. The GDG concluded that the risk of harm from traction outweighed its benefits and made a conditional recommendation against its use. This decision was driven by indirect evidence of potential harms and the lack of observed benefits in sham-controlled trials.
